bib.title: InfMem: Learning System-2 Memory Control for Long-Context Agent

legacy_report:
NOTE FIRST: this PDF is InfMem, not MemAgent. MemAgent (Yu et al., 2025) is the baseline it improves on. Cite it as a successor/critique of MemAgent, not as the MemAgent source.

COVERAGE: all 33 pages read (112,001 chars): body, appendices A-F, tables, case studies. References skimmed. No "Limitations" section exists. No embedded instructions. The abstract's code link is a placeholder ("/githubcode").

SOURCE: "InfMem: Learning System-2 Memory Control for Long-Context Agent". Xinyu Wang* (McGill), Mingze Li* (Noah's Ark Lab), Peng Lu (Université de Montréal), Xiao-Wen Chang (McGill), Lifeng Shang, Jinpeng Li, Fei Mi, Prasanna Parthasarathi, Yufei Cui (corresponding; all Noah's Ark Lab). Preprint, arXiv 2602.02704v2, 7 Aug 2026. No venue stated.

MAIN CLAIM: MemAgent streams chunks and overwrites a fixed-size memory in the same way at every step. It cannot tell whether the memory is already sufficient, cannot revisit text it has passed, and cannot stop early. InfMem adds a PRETHINK -> RETRIEVE -> WRITE loop over the same bounded memory:
- PRETHINK sees only (question, memory) and emits STOP or SEARCH, plus a query and top-k.
- RETRIEVE runs BM25 over the same document (past or future), with no external corpus.
- WRITE jointly compresses (memory, current chunk, retrieved text) under the budget.
- Training is SFT distilled from Qwen3-32B, then GRPO with rewards for correctness, early stopping, and protocol validity.

HEADLINE NUMBERS
1. Abstract: "+10.17, +11.84, and +8.23 points on Qwen3-1.7B, Qwen3-4B, and Qwen2.5-7B", with latency reduced "3.9× on average (up to 5.1×)".
   - Setup: InfMem vs MemAgent, average over benchmarks. The 5.1x is for Qwen3-4B at 1M context.
   - Latency figure (p.9): 128 test samples per task, 4×H100, vLLM.
   - Caveat: the 5.1x is the best case. The default "3-stop" policy (stop after 3 consecutive STOPs) is slower than "1-stop" but more accurate.
2. Table 1 (p.7), 1M tokens, Qwen3-4B+RL, synthetic distractor-padded benchmarks, 128 samples per task:
   - MuSiQue: InfMem 56.86 vs MemAgent 35.91.
   - 2Wiki: 66.39 vs 35.18.
   - SQuAD gap is small (73.81 vs 77.74, where MemAgent is higher at 1M).
   - Average over lengths, Qwen3-4B+RL: HQA 66.40 vs 54.56. Qwen2.5-7B+RL: HQA 60.30 vs 52.07.
   - Without RL (Qwen3-4B, HQA average): InfMem 50.25 vs MemAgent 43.61.
3. Tokens decoded per query (Table 3, p.9), Qwen3-4B:
   - At 896k: InfMem 33,085, MemAgent 117,418, Mem-α 114,992.
   - From 800 to 6400 length units: InfMem cost grows about 5×, MemAgent about 11×.
4. LongBench QA F1 average (Table 2, p.8):
   - Qwen3-4B+RL: InfMem 50.93 vs MemAgent+RL 47.11.
   - Qwen3-1.7B+RL: 41.54 vs 35.90.
   - Qwen2.5-7B+RL: 46.46 vs 40.01.
   - Qwen2.5-7B, no RL: MemAgent 39.33 beats InfMem 36.85.
   - InfMem is also below the YaRN baseline on Qasper for 1.7B and 4B without RL.

Table 8 (p.23), with at most 128 samples per task: InfMem's average performance is 64.85 vs 56.94 for MemAgent NoThink-RL, with a similar preserved-answer rate (69.77% vs 69.53%). Appendix F.1 (p.25-26): zero-shot on Gemma-4-E4B-IT, InfMem beats MemAgent in all 8 task-length configurations (+9.1 to +24.1 F1). Both are untrained there.

QUOTES
- p.2: "every chunk is forced through the same fixed-size memory bottleneck, regardless of the complexity of the underlying question."
- p.7: "MemAgent's recurrent architecture is highly susceptible to gradual information loss over extended horizons."
- p.3: MemAgent "cannot assess memory sufficiency, revisit lost context, or terminate early."
- p.10 conclusion: "the primary bottleneck shifts from raw memory capacity to cognitive control".

LIMITS / NOT SHOWN
- The comparison is not like-for-like on input (p.18). Output length and steps were matched, not the input or memory budget. InfMem gets up to 4k extra retrieved tokens per step, which the authors say forces more compression into memory. It also uses a BM25 index over the whole document, which MemAgent does not. Working memory: 5k-token chunk plus a 1k-token memory slot (p.28).
- The authors disabled MemAgent's thinking mode on Qwen3 (Appendix E).
- All benchmarks are synthetic: gold documents inserted once, plus same-corpus distractors. Only 128 samples per task, and no variance or confidence intervals are reported.
- LongBench is the only natural-distribution test, and InfMem does not win every cell there.
- Only small Qwen backbones (1.7B, 4B, 7B) with Qwen3-32B as teacher; Gemma-4 was tested zero-shot only. No frontier models.
- The early-stop reward uses an exact-match check on the memory, which the authors admit "may occasionally misjudge" (p.6).
- The 1M tests are padded text, so it is unclear how this transfers to real documents.
- The paper does not compare against MemAgent given the same BM25 retrieval tool as an equal-budget ablation. It does not isolate how much of the gain comes from retrieval versus the stop control, apart from the 1-stop vs 3-stop variants.

BUILDS ON
- MemAgent (Yu et al., 2025): the baseline and problem setup (chunked streaming, overwrite memory, RL-trained).
- MemGPT (Packer et al., 2023), MEM1 (Zhou et al., 2025), Memory-R1 (Yan et al., 2025), Mem-α (Wang et al., 2025c).
- Compared against: YaRN (Peng et al., 2024), RAG (Lewis et al., 2020), RESP (Jiang et al., 2025), Search-R1 (Jin et al., 2025), Self-RAG (Asai et al., 2024).
- GRPO for RL; dual-process framing from Kahneman (2011); Sumers et al. (2023).
- RULER-style/NIAH data construction follows MemAgent.

FIGURE CANDIDATES
- Figure 1 (p.3): the PRETHINK-RETRIEVE-WRITE loop over bounded memory. Algorithm 1 (p.4) is the same loop in pseudocode.
- Figure 2 (p.9): accuracy vs context length (64K-1M) and accuracy vs latency at 1M. This is the best single picture of "control beats passive overwrite".
- Figure 6 (p.18): before/after RL memory writes, showing wrong vs correct bridging.
